trails.trailTip: Alligators often rest right beside or under the boardwalk in the dry season — stay on the boardwalk, keep a respectful distance, and never feed them; it's illegal and dangerous.
trails.didYouKnow: The boardwalk sits atop a natural alligator hole that stays wet even during the driest months, concentrating wildlife nearby.

trails.trailTip: Most visitors bike or take the tram rather than walk the full 15 miles; there's no shade on the loop, so bring sun protection and plenty of water regardless of how you cover it.
trails.didYouKnow: Despite its name, no sharks live in Shark Valley — it's named for the sawgrass slough that drains toward the historic Shark River.

trails.trailTip: The elevated boardwalk offers one of the best sunrise or sunset views of the sawgrass prairie in the park, with little foot traffic to compete for the view.
trails.didYouKnow: Pa-hay-okee means 'grassy waters' in Seminole, the same phrase behind the Everglades' nickname, the 'River of Grass.'

trails.trailTip: This shaded hammock loop is a good midday option when other, more exposed trails feel hot.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail is named for the gumbo limbo tree, nicknamed the 'tourist tree' for its reddish, peeling bark.

trails.trailTip: Mosquitoes can be intense here, especially in wet season (roughly May-Oct), so bring repellent.
trails.didYouKnow: The boardwalk winds through one of the largest mangrove forests in the Western Hemisphere.

trails.trailTip: Keep an eye out for barred owls and tree snails in the dense canopy along this shaded loop.
trails.didYouKnow: The hammock shelters the largest living mahogany tree in the United States.

trails.trailTip: You may notice charred bark on some pines — prescribed burns here mimic the natural fire cycle this habitat depends on.
trails.didYouKnow: Pine rockland habitat depends on periodic fire to clear underbrush and let pine seedlings take root.

trails.trailTip: The open pineland offers little shade, so this trail is best hiked or biked in cooler months and earlier in the day.
trails.didYouKnow: The pine rockland here is one of the most fire-dependent and imperiled habitats in Florida.

trails.estimatedTime: 1 day round trip (day hike) / overnight backcountry trip
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, an overnight backcountry permit from the Flamingo area (reservable on recreation.gov up to 90 days ahead) is required to camp at the Coastal Prairie site, though a day hike without camping only needs the standard park entrance fee.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail follows an old cotton-plantation-era road bed through a landscape shaped by salt spray and periodic hurricanes.

animals.whereToLook: Anhinga Trail boardwalk and Shark Valley canals
animals.viewingTip: Stay on the boardwalk and view alligators from several feet above the water — never feed them (it's illegal and makes them dangerously bold around people) and keep small children and pets well back from the water's edge at all times.
animals.didYouKnow: Alligators concentrate in deeper 'gator holes' during the winter dry season, which is also when they're easiest for visitors to spot.

animals.whereToLook: Brackish coastal waters near the Flamingo marina
animals.viewingTip: American crocodiles are shier than alligators and nest in coastal sand or marl mounds each spring — watch from the Flamingo marina or a boat with binoculars, and never approach a nesting mound or a basking crocodile for a closer photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Everglades National Park is one of the only places on Earth where American alligators and American crocodiles live side by side.

animals.whereToLook: Pine rockland and hardwood hammock edges near Long Pine Key, most often only as tracks
animals.viewingTip: A Florida panther sighting is extremely rare and usually just tracks in soft ground — if you're fortunate enough to see one, stay in your vehicle or keep well back, make noise to avoid surprising it, and never approach, corner, or try to follow one of the fewer than 200 individuals left in the wild.
animals.didYouKnow: The Florida panther is the official state animal, and its population has slowly rebounded from fewer than 30 individuals in the 1990s.

animals.whereToLook: Coastal marshes near Eco Pond and Mrazek Pond
animals.viewingTip: Spoonbills feed by sweeping their bills through shallow water — watch from a pond overlook or road shoulder with binoculars rather than wading in to get closer, since flushing a feeding flock wastes energy the birds need for the season.
animals.didYouKnow: A roseate spoonbill's pink color comes from pigments in the crustaceans it eats, much like a flamingo's.

animals.whereToLook: Flamingo marina and canals near the coast
animals.viewingTip: Watch manatees surface to breathe from a dock or the marina, approaching slowly and quietly if you're in a boat — touching, feeding, or chasing a manatee is illegal and can separate calves from mothers or injure the animal.
animals.didYouKnow: Manatees have no natural predators as adults but are frequently injured by boat strikes, which is why speed zones protect them near the coast.

animals.whereToLook: Cypress domes and wading-bird rookeries near Pa-hay-okee and Mrazek Pond
animals.viewingTip: Wood storks nest colonially in cypress domes — view any rookery from a boardwalk or established overlook with binoculars rather than walking off-trail toward the trees, since flushing nesting adults can expose eggs and chicks to sun and predators.
animals.didYouKnow: Wood storks time their nesting to the Everglades' dry season, when shrinking water levels concentrate fish into easy-to-catch pools.

animals.whereToLook: Perched with wings spread to dry along the Anhinga Trail boardwalk
animals.viewingTip: Anhingas often perch at arm's length from the boardwalk railing — enjoy the close view on the bird's own terms, but never reach out, corner it, or crowd around a single bird, since these are wild animals habituated to the boardwalk, not tame ones.
animals.didYouKnow: Anhingas lack the oil glands most waterbirds use to waterproof their feathers, which is why they must spread their wings to dry after diving.

animals.whereToLook: Roadsides and levees, especially near Long Pine Key, at dawn or after rain
animals.viewingTip: Burmese pythons are a destructive invasive species, but they should still only be reported to park staff or the official python removal program rather than approached or handled by visitors — large constrictors can injure someone who tries to grab or corner them.
animals.didYouKnow: Burmese pythons, likely introduced through the exotic pet trade, have caused steep declines in the park's rabbit, raccoon, and deer populations.

animals.whereToLook: Sawgrass marshes near Shark Valley and the Pa-hay-okee overlook, hunting apple snails
animals.viewingTip: Snail kites hunt low over open marsh for apple snails — watch their distinctive flight with binoculars from the road or a boardwalk rather than wading into the marsh to get closer, which disturbs both the birds and the wetland habitat.
animals.didYouKnow: The snail kite's hooked bill is precisely shaped to extract apple snails from their shells, a food source it depends on almost exclusively.
